items.quote: A head mounted augmented reality design practice for maintenance assembly: Toward meeting perceptual and cognitive needs of AR users

items.field: Authors
items.value: Dedy Ariansyah, John Ahmet Erkoyuncu, Iveta Eimontaite, Teegan Johnson, Anne-Marie Oostveen, Sarah Fletcher, Sarah Sharples

items.field: Stated objective/approach
items.value: Uses a theoretically-driven approach to interaction design to investigate the impact of different AR modalities in terms of information mode (video vs. 3D animation) and interaction modality (hand-gesture vs. voice command) on user performance, workload, eye gaze behaviours, and usability during a maintenance assembly task
items.quote: This paper uses a theoretically-driven approach to interaction design to investigate the impact of different AR modalities in terms of information mode (i.e. video vs. 3D animation) and interaction modality (i.e. hand-gesture vs. voice command) on user performance, workload, eye gaze behaviours, and usability during a maintenance assembly task.

items.field: Key result: 3D animation vs. video instructions in task completion time
items.value: 14% improvement over the video instructions in task completion time (3D animation led to improvement)
items.quote: in particular, 3D animation led to a 14% improvement over the video instructions in task completion time.

citations.quote: in particular, 3D animation led to a 14% improvement over the video instructions in task completion time.
the 3D animation-based instruction show a significantly faster completion time (14%) compared to a video-based visualisation.

items.field: Key result: eye gaze behaviours and AR modalities
items.value: Insights from eye gaze behaviours such as number of fixations and transition between AOIs revealed differences in attention switching and task comprehension difficulty with the choice of AR modalities
items.quote: insights from eye gaze behaviours such as number of fixations and transition between Areas of Interest (AOIs) revealed the differences in attention switching and task comprehension difficulty with the choice of AR modalities.

items.field: Key result: subjective user perceptions and ergonomic issues
items.value: Subjective user perceptions highlight ergonomic issues such as misguidance and over-reliance, to be considered from the joint cognitive systems (JCSs) perspective and in line with Multiple Resources Model predictions
items.quote: While, subjective user perceptions highlight some ergonomic issues such as misguidance and over-reliance, which must be considered and addressed from the joint cognitive systems' (JCSs) perspective and in line with the predictions derived from the Multiple Resources Model.

items.field: Stated limitation: limited research on user interaction with AR interfaces
items.value: Limited research has been done to understand user interaction with AR interfaces, which may lead to poor usability, risk of occupational hazards, and low acceptance of AR systems
items.quote: However, limited research has been done to understand user interaction with AR interfaces, which may lead to poor usability, risk of occupational hazards, and low acceptance of AR systems.

items.field: Stated challenge: perceiving virtual and real objects simultaneously
items.value: Combining digital and physical spaces so users can perceive and comprehend both virtual and real objects simultaneously while doing one or more real world tasks is challenging
items.quote: combining both digital and physical spaces in a way that enables users to perceive and comprehend both virtual and real objects simultaneously while doing one or more real world tasks is challenging (Gabbard et al., 2019).

items.field: Stated objective
items.value: This paper aims to provide a theoretically driven approach based on the Multiple Resource Model (MRM) (Wickens, 2002, 2008) and the JCS’s perspective (Hollnagel, 2005) to the design practice for AR modalities.
items.quote: This paper aims to provide a theoretically driven approach based on the Multiple Resource Model (MRM) (Wickens, 2002, 2008) and the JCS ’ s perspective (Hollnagel, 2005) to the design practice for AR mo - dalities.

items.value: This study considers the information mode and input interface for the implementation on HMD.

items.field: Application considered
items.value: Industrial assembly for manufacturing and maintenance
items.quote: The application considered is in industrial assembly for manufacturing and maintenance, as these design principles have to be identified in specific domains and fields prior to generalisation across a broader context (Hollnagel, 2005).

items.field: Performance comparison baseline
items.value: Paper-based manual

items.quote: In addition, this study also recorded and analysed eye gaze behaviours and user perception to capture possible factors that contribute to a variation in performance and user safety, aspects that are rarely considered in the evaluation of AR usability in manufacturing and maintenance application.

items.field: Stated limitation — voice command interaction: ambient noise may reduce effectiveness
items.value: Main hindrance of using voice command could be ambient noise, which may reduce the effectiveness of this interaction mode

items.field: Stated limitation — animation information mode: occlusion, improper brightness (poor visibility), and inaccurate overlay could lead to confusion and cognitive demand
items.value: Occlusion, improper brightness of the animation (i.e. poor visibility), and inaccurate overlay could lead to confusion and place a cognitive demand on understanding the required task

items.field: Stated limitation — AR headset comfort for prolonged use and aspects needing improvement (field of view, heated surface after long usage, rendering quality)

Some other aspects that need further improvement according to the partici - pants are Field of View, heated surface after long usage, and rendering quality.

items.field: Key result: effect of interaction mode (hand gesture vs voice command) on task performance
items.value: Interaction mode did not affect the performance gain; no effect of distinct interaction modes was found for the number of errors.
items.quote: Taken all this, this study found that the interaction mode did not affect the performance gain whereas type of information mode caused variations in the task performance (i.e. time completion and accuracy).

items.field: Key result: performance gain between hand gesture (air press button) and voice command in navigating task instructions
items.value: Significant performance gain between hand gesture (air press button) and voice command in navigating the instructions for the given task; not sufficiently manifested in performance benefits for hand gesture despite more resource allocations in MRM.
items.quote: 15 significant performance gain between hand gesture (i.e. air press button) and voice command in navigating the instructions for the given task.

items.field: Key result: number of task errors, AR vs paper-based manuals, 3D animation-based visualisation only
items.value: Number of task errors was significantly reduced when using AR compared to paper-based manuals, but only for the 3D animation-based visualisation.
items.quote: Furthermore, this study also found that the number of task errors was significantly reduced when using AR compared to paper-based manuals but only for the 3D animation-based visualisation.

items.field: Key result: number of mistakes, video-based vs 3D animation-based instructions
items.value: Participants who used video-based instructions made significantly more mistakes than those who experienced 3D animation-based instructions.
items.quote: It was also found that participants who used video-based instructions made significantly more mistakes than those who experienced 3D animation-based instructions.

items.field: Key result: effect of information mode on task performance
items.value: Type of information mode caused variations in task performance (i.e. time completion and accuracy).
items.quote: Taken all this, this study found that the interaction mode did not affect the performance gain whereas type of information mode caused variations in the task performance (i.e. time completion and accuracy).

items.field: Key result: subjective workload overall between AR and Non-AR approaches and information mode
items.value: No statistical evidence of workload difference.
items.quote: Whilst performance increment and variation were apparent between both the AR and Non-AR approaches as well as the information mode, the measure of subjective workload did not reveal any statistical evidence on the account of workload difference.

items.field: Key result: within-subject analysis for paper-based manual workload after AR experience
items.value: Statistically significant difference for Mental, Physical, Effort, and Total workload after experiencing the AR assistance systems.
items.quote: Nevertheless, the comparison of within-subject analyses for the paper-based manual showed a statistically significant difference for Mental, Physical, Effort, and Total workload after they experienced the AR assistance systems.

items.field: Key result: HR, paper-based manual vs Animation-Hand (AH) group
items.value: All AR conditions elicited a higher level of HR compared to a paper-based manual (Table 5); significant result observed only between the paper-based manual group and the Animation-Hand (AH) group.
items.quote: In particular, all AR conditions elicited a higher level of HR compared to a paper-based manual (Table 5) with the significant result observed only between the paper-based manual group and the Animation-Hand (AH) group.

items.field: Key result: total dwell time, dynamic graphical vs textual or static graphical instructions
items.value: Participants spent more time interpreting and relating dynamic graphical instructions (e.g. animation and video) than textual instructions or static graphical instructions, indicated by significant difference in total dwell time.
items.quote: The analysis of eye movement revealed that participants spent more time interpreting and relating dynamic graphical instructions (e.g. animation and video) than textual instructions or static graphical instructions, which was indicated by the significant difference in total dwell time.

items.field: Key result: total number of fixations, dynamic graphical vs static instructions
items.value: Significant difference in total number of fixations; participants processed a larger amount of information from dynamic graphical information.
items.quote: Moreover, the significant difference in the total number of fixations signifies that participants processed a larger amount of information from the dynamic graphical information.

items.field: Key result: eye information search transitions in video-based instruction
items.value: No significant difference between Video-Video and Video-tool, Video-Video and Video-SubInstruction, Video-Video and Gearbox-Video.
items.quote: This is indicated by no significant difference between Video-Video and Video-tool, Video-Video and Video-SubInstruction, Video-Video and Gearbox-Video.

items.field: Key result: eye information search transitions in animation-based instruction
items.value: Significant difference between Gearbox-Gearbox and Gearbox-SubInstruction, Gearbox-Tool, and Gearbox-Tool.
items.quote: In contrast, there was a significant difference between Gearbox-Gearbox and Gearbox-SubInstruction, Gearbox-Tool, and Gearbox-Tool in animation-based instruction, which may suggest that overlaying 3D animation directly over the gearbox comprised enough information to perform the required task.

items.field: Key result: time looking at video and gearbox vs animation and gearbox
items.value: Equivalent amount of time.
items.quote: The results show that the amount of time users spent looking at the video and gearbox was equivalent to the total time spent looking at the animation and gearbox.

items.field: Key result: total number of fixations, video plus gearbox vs animation plus gearbox
items.value: Total number of fixations was significantly greater in the sum of the video and gearbox than in animation and gearbox.
items.quote: Nonetheless, the total number of fixations was significantly greater in the sum of the video and gearbox than in animation and gearbox.

items.field: Key result: Fixation Rate, video vs animation
items.value: Significantly higher ratio of video than animation.
items.quote: Besides, the Fixation Rate indicated a significant higher ratio of video than animation, which may imply higher complexity in information decoding.

items.field: Key result: correlation between total number of fixations and completion time in both conditions
items.value: Significant correlation in both conditions; fixations frequency could be a good predictor of task completion time.
items.quote: Moreover, the significant correlation between the total number of fixations and the completion time in both conditions revealed that fixations frequency could be a good predictor of task completion time

items.field: Stated limitation: physically demanding task with both hands
items.value: A difference would likely be apparent when the task involves a highly physically demanding task, which requires both hands in the operation as noted in the subjective feedback.
items.quote: It is likely that a difference would be apparent when the task involves a highly physically demanding task, which requires both hands in the operation as noted in the subjective feedback.

items.field: Stated technical limitation: non-task-related workload in AR
items.value: AR can also induce non-task related workload as indicated by physiological responses, associated with increased engagement in solving manual tasks.
items.quote: However, AR can also induce non-task related workload as indicated by their physiological responses, which is associated with the increased engagement in solving manual tasks.

items.field: Stated research question (fourth question) addressed by AR conditions findings
items.value: Participants liked to use AR as a novel way of interacting with information required to perform an assembly task.
items.quote: Considering all AR conditions, the findings address the fourth question, namely participants liked to use AR as a novel way of interacting with information required to perform an assembly task.

items.field: Key result: Perceived usability across AR modalities
items.value: Not statistically significantly different.
items.quote: Perceived usability was not statistically significantly different across AR modalities.

items.field: Key result: Number of errors and association with eye tracking metrics
items.value: Errors were not marked by any association with the eye tracking metrics used in this study.
items.quote: Although the number of errors were not marked by any association with the eye tracking metrics used in this study, there are some evidences that eye tracking metrics (e.g. number of fixations) could discriminate different user strategies to interact with different information modes, and their impacts on the task performance.

items.field: Information mode limitation: Video-based instruction presentation and attention shift
items.value: Presentation limited to one perspective; attention shift from video to task requires head movement, increasing workload and frequent head movements that could lead to fatigue or neck pain in complex and long assembly tasks.
items.quote: In the video-based instruction, the presentation of the information is limited to one perspective.

items.field: Information mode limitation: Safety-related issue with video
items.value: Participants tended to focus attention on the video instead of the component while performing assembly and disassembly, potentially leading to occupational hazards and physical injuries.
items.quote: Further, there is a safety-related issue with the use of video as the information mode. During the maintenance task, participants tended to focus their attention on the video instead of on the component while performing the assembly and disassembly process.

items.field: Information mode limitation: 3D animation misalignment, brightness and occlusion
items.value: Misaligned overlay can introduce confusion; occlusion of the real object by the 3D animation blocks the user's view when searching for relevant parts; improper occlusion due to poor brightness may cause misunderstanding of spatial properties, incorrect operation, and increased eye strain.
items.quote: the presentation of 3D animation right on the equipment could introduce confusion when the overlay is misaligned with the physical component.

items.field: Interaction mode result: Voice commands
items.value: Participants found voice commands could help them concentrate on the task better and complete the task quicker if both hands are busy.
items.quote: participants found that voice commands could help them concentrate on the task better and complete the task quicker if both their hands are busy.

items.field: Interaction mode result: Hand-gesture
items.value: Use of hand-gesture may be tiring due to the need to raise and lower the hand when interacting with the interface.
items.quote: The use of hand-gesture may be tiring due to the need to raise and to lower the hand when interacting with interface.

items.field: Hardware result: Hololens 2 comfort
items.value: Participants found the Hololens 2 comfortable and not too heavy for the task duration tested.
items.quote: participants found that the Hololens 2 was comfortable and not too heavy for the task duration tested.

items.field: Stated limitation: Simplicity of maintenance tasks and generalisability
items.value: Maintenance tasks were relatively simple and limited (Allen key to (un)screw bolts and simple hand movements); questionable whether results could be generalised to a more complex assembly task such as an aircraft cable assembly task.
items.quote: Firstly, the maintenance tasks tested in this study were relatively simple and limited, consisting of the use of an Allen key to (un)screw bolts and simple hand movements to perform the assembly and disassembly process. It is therefore questionable whether this result could be generalised for a more complex assembly task such as an aircraft cable assembly task.

items.field: Stated limitation: Imprecise AR overlay in high-precision tasks
items.value: A slight misalignment of 3D animation was still comprehensible for AR users, but whether this holds for assembly tasks requiring more precision in tracking and registration of virtual objects to real components (such as spacecraft cable assembly) is questioned; further research should investigate imprecise overlay on complex assembly tasks and optimal information mode.
items.quote: In the current study, a slight misalignment of 3D animation was still comprehensible for the AR users, but the question arises whether this would still be the case with assembly tasks that require more precision in terms of tracking and registration of virtual objects to real components such as in spacecraft cable assembly.

items.field: Stated limitation: Task duration and environment not reflecting real industrial setting
items.value: Task duration and environment may not be sufficient to reflect a real industrial setting that can be noisy, with poor lighting and exposure to time pressure, which may impact efficacy of information and interaction mode.
items.quote: Secondly, the task duration and environment considered in the present study may not be sufficient to reflect a real industrial setting that can be noisy, with poor lighting as well as exposure to time pressure. These factors may have impact on the efficacy of information and interaction mode.

items.field: Key result: information mode — 3D animation vs video-based instructions, task completion time
items.value: 3D animation could help to achieve faster task completion times compared to video-based instructions
items.quote: The findings show that 3D animation could help to achieve faster task completion times and fewer errors in guiding task assembly compared to video-based in - structions.

items.field: Key result: information mode — 3D animation vs video-based instructions, errors
items.value: 3D animation could help to achieve fewer errors compared to video-based instructions
items.quote: The findings show that 3D animation could help to achieve faster task completion times and fewer errors in guiding task assembly compared to video-based in - structions.

items.value: Participants indicated a high acceptance of video usage

items.quote: Regarding the video-based instruction, although participants indicated a high acceptance of video usage, the eye movement analysis showed inefficient scanning behav - iour when processing the information, which is likely, contribute to task performance.

items.value: Voice command might not be effective in a noisy environment
items.quote: Concerning the interaction mode, voice command is perceived as useful when the task at hand requires the use of both hands though it might not be effective in a noisy environ - ment.

items.field: Key result: interaction mode — voice command, physical strain

items.quote: Besides, it could alleviate physical strain when the maintenance task is physically demanding.

items.field: Stated limitation: 3D animation may cause confusion or misguided information
items.value: 3D animation could cause confusion to the users and possibly provide misguided information when the registration is misaligned, and the brightness and occlusion are not appropriately designed
items.quote: Nevertheless, the use of 3D animation could cause confusion to the users and possibly, provide misguided in - formation when the registration is misaligned, and the brightness and occlusion are not appropriately designed.

items.field: Stated limitation: video-based instruction occupational hazards
items.value: Video usage could introduce occupational hazards if the user is not warned to focus their attention on the equipment while doing the required task
items.quote: Furthermore, video usage could introduce occupational hazards if the user is not warned to focus their attention on the equip - ment while doing the required task.

items.field: Stated limitation: AR tracking and registration robustness
items.value: AR tracking and registration were still not without flaws even in the laboratory setting and should be improved, especially for industrial contexts
items.quote: From the technological side, the AR tracking and registration were still not without flaws even in the labo - ratory setting. Therefore, the robustness of AR tracking and registration is also critical and should be improved, especially for the implementa - tion in the industrial contexts where the environment is relatively more complex.

items.field: Stated limitation: transferability of design practices across applications
items.value: It is questionable to what extent the design practices are transferable across different applications (e.g. medical)
items.quote: It is also questionable to what extent the design practices are transferable across different applications (e.g. medical).
